newsitem.title: USA: Let the net be your guide to landing a summer job.
newsitem.headline: Let the net be your guide to landing a summer job.

text.p: It's not too late to land a summer job, if you know where to look.

The Internet offers a modest but growing batch of Web sites advertising seasonal employment for high school and college students, and education workers looking to supplement their school-year income with summertime work.
Jobs listed online range from running a snack-shop cash register in Bryce Canyon National Park in Utah to lifeguarding in the Poconos to fixing rental bikes on Kiawah Island Resort in South Carolina.
Summer job Web sites join dozens of more general career and employment Web sites that include seasonal, temporary and part-time work mixed in with full-time and permanent listings.

Many employers already have filled their summer slots, but that shouldn't discourage late comers, said Susan Greenberg, co-creator of Petersen's Great Summer Jobs (http://www.greatsummerjobs.com), a list of close to 6,000 camp jobs for high-school and college students.
"Anybody great could get a job in a minute because we're coming up to the (hiring) deadline," Greenberg said.

Petersen, best known for its printed college guides, started Great Summer Jobs two years ago after publishing an online directory of summer camps for kids. The first summer, about 30 camps participated. Today, 167 camps pay Petersen a small fee to advertise jobs in 600 categories. Petersen doesn't track the number of jobs filled from its Web page, but Greenberg said much of the feedback she receives is positive, exemplified by one Long Island day-camp director who began advertising in December and by March had hired almost his entire summer crew through the Web site.

Camp Sequoia, a sleep-over camp in New York's Catskill Mountains recruited five or six of its summer staff of 150 counsellors by advertising in the "Camp Jobs" section of the Kidscamp (http://www.kidscamp.com) Web site. Though small, the number is significant "because we do a lot of recruiting across the country," said Brian Crug, the camp's staff recruiter.
Kidscamp creators Nancy Diamond and Kim Bregman added camp jobs listings to their 18-month-old camp Web site once they realised how many college and high school students were Internet savvy.
"They go to school with their laptops and use the Net not just to research papers but to look for jobs too," Diamond said. "Camps are recognising this is a terrific way to market themselves."
Camp jobs aren't the only summer situations advertised online.

SummerJobs.com (http://www.summerjobs.com), a Web site run by Fishnet NewMedia in Bourne, Mass., lists about 500 jobs including openings for computer programmers, nannies, secretaries, and waiters. Although most people who visit are 18 to 24 years old, it's also popular with educators looking to earn some extra cash during the summer, said Donna Donovan, Fishnet owner.

The online jobs database at Cool Works (http://www.coolworks.com) includes positions with national parks, cruise ships, camps, resorts, ranches, and state parks, as well as volunteer positions and winter-time ski jobs. A "Help Wanted Now" section is updated weekly.
Cool Works founder Bill Berg started the site after spending nine years recruiting students for seasonal jobs in Yellowstone.

Recruiting the old-fashioned way "involves a whole lot of printing, postage and patience," Berg writes on the Web site. "It's labour and resource intensive. The Web looks to me to be a nice way to give the scoop on seasonal jobs without having to wait for the mail and without all of that paper being hauled around the country in trucks and planes."

If you know how to look, it's possible to find summer jobs on sites that don't specifically advertise seasonal openings. For example, CareerPath, a Web site that lists hundreds of thousands of help wanted ads from 32 local and regional newspapers, lets visitors search for keywords such as "intern" or "summer" to turn up temporary paid or unpaid positions.
Other resources include:

-- America's Job Bank (http://www.ajb.dni.us) -- A computerized network of listings from state employment agencies currently offers 87 "seasonal" jobs including excursion boat bartender in Deep River, Conn., and fire lookout in Calaveras County, Calif.

-- Local Resources (http://www.jobtrack.com/jobguide/local.html) -- An extensive, state-by-state list compiled by Margaret Riley, consultant and author of "The Guide to Internet Job Searching." Included are Web sites, newsgroups, links to local newspaper classified ads, state-run job banks and positions with companies.
-- Overseas Jobs.com (http://www.overseasjobs.com) -- Seasonal and full-time jobs in various countries and categories including engineering, arts, sales and training.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
